passage:
"Appa, it's ruined!" Lavanya held up her worksheet. A hole gaped where she had rubbed out the number seven for the fifth time.
"Let me see. Oh, the eraser won."
"It's not funny! Ma'am will think I'm careless. I'm not handing it in."
"Did you get the sum right?"
"Yes, but the seven was wonky."
"A wonky seven and the right answer." Tarun sat down beside her. "You know what I did at work today? Sent an email to the wrong person. The whole team saw."
"What did you do?"
"Said sorry and sent it again. Mistakes are how I learn what to check."
Lavanya sniffed. "But you're a grown-up."
"Grown-ups learn the same way. Want to tape the hole and write 'eraser accident' next to it?"
A small smile. "Can I draw the eraser?"

qa.q: How many times had Lavanya rubbed out the seven?
qa.a: She had rubbed it out for the fifth time.

qa.q: What was Lavanya worried about when she refused to hand in the worksheet?
qa.a: She was worried her teacher would think she was careless because of one wonky seven.

qa.q: What turning point helped Lavanya calm down?
qa.a: Tarun shared his own mistake at work and said mistakes are how he learns, then offered a funny way to fix the hole.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel watching Lavanya cry over a wonky seven?
qa.a: He may feel worried and tender, which is why he stays gentle and shares his own mistake.

grounding: A girl rubs out work until the paper tears and refuses to hand it in, and her father shows that mistakes are part of learning.

passage: My name is Sonali. In class five I used to cry if my handwriting had one smudge. Once I rewrote my Hindi essay four times and rubbed so hard the page tore, so I hid it in my bag and told Ramesh sir I'd forgotten it. He found out. I thought he'd be angry. Instead he showed me his own old notebook from school, full of crossings-out and a big ink blot. "This boy became a teacher," he said. "Mistakes show you where to look next." After that I handed in my essay with one smudge on it. My heart was thumping. He gave it a star anyway.

qa.q: How many times did Sonali rewrite the Hindi essay?
qa.a: Sonali rewrote it four times.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid of when Ramesh sir found out about the essay?
qa.a: Sonali was afraid he would be angry.

qa.q: What did Ramesh sir choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: He showed his own messy school notebook and said mistakes show where to look next, which made Sonali brave enough to hand in imperfect work.

qa.q: How might Ramesh sir have felt seeing the essay with one smudge?
qa.a: He was probably pleased and proud of Sonali's courage, which is why he gave it a star.

grounding: A child who cried at small errors and hid a torn essay learns from a teacher that mistakes are part of how learning works.

passage: In the Andheri flat, Leela had been rubbing out the same letter in her Hindi copy for ten minutes. Rub, write, rub. Suddenly the page ripped, a jagged hole right through her homework. She burst into tears. "Now it's ruined! I can't take it to school like this. Ma'am will think I'm careless." Her mother, Vinita, put down the vegetables and sat beside her. Leela's shoulders were shaking. "It was only one letter," Vinita said softly. "Remember when you learnt to swim? You swallowed so much water first." Leela sniffed. "That's different." "Is it? Mistakes are how you learnt." Leela stared at the torn page, hiccupping, not yet convinced.

qa.q: How long had Leela been rubbing out the same letter?
qa.a: For ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Leela afraid of when the page ripped?
qa.a: She was scared that the torn page meant failure and that Ma'am would think she was careless.

qa.q: How could Vinita keep helping Leela with mistakes?
qa.a: Keep reminding her gently that mistakes are how learning works, like swimming, and let her hand in imperfect work.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to see Leela cry over one letter?
qa.a: Vinita likely feels worried and tender, seeing how much a tiny error hurts her daughter.

grounding: Shows a child who rubs out work until it tears and cries at a small error, and a parent saying mistakes are how learning happens.

passage:
"Asif, time to hand in the drawings."
"I can't, Madhav-sir. The sun is wrong."
"The sun looks lovely."
"It's not round. One side is flat. I'll do it again at home."
"You've started this one four times today. Look, the paper's gone thin."
Asif's chin wobbled. "If it's not perfect, it's bad."
"Can I show you something?" Madhav-sir opened his own sketchbook. "This horse. I drew the legs wrong three times. See the smudges?"
"But you're a teacher."
"Teachers learn by making mistakes too. That's how the legs got better."
Asif looked at the flat sun. A tear dripped onto the paper. "Can I hand it in with a note that says 'sun wrong'?"
"You can. I'd love to see it."

qa.q: How many times had Asif started the drawing that day?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Asif's chin wobble?
qa.a: He felt upset and afraid, believing that any flaw made his drawing bad.

qa.q: What did Madhav-sir do that helped Asif?
qa.a: He showed his own smudged horse and said teachers learn by making mistakes too.

qa.q: What might Madhav-sir be thinking when Asif asks to add a note?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and pleased that Asif is willing to hand in imperfect work.

grounding: Illustrates a child who restarts work and refuses to hand it in unless perfect, helped by a teacher who shares his own mistakes.

passage: Last year I cried over a spelling test where I got nine out of ten. Zubin got six and was cheerful all day. I didn't understand how. I'm Madhav, and I used to rub things out so many times my notebooks had holes. I wouldn't hand in my science project because one label was crooked, and Ma'am gave me a zero for not handing it in, which was worse than crooked. Then Zubin showed me his cricket bat, full of dents. "Every dent is a ball I missed," he said, "and now I hit them." That stuck with me. I still hate mistakes. But now I hand things in, even crooked ones.

qa.q: What score did Madhav get on the spelling test?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel about the crooked label?
qa.a: Madhav felt that one flaw meant failure, so the project felt too shameful to hand in.

qa.q: What lesson helped Madhav change?
qa.a: Zubin's dented bat showed that misses are how you learn to hit, so Madhav started handing work in.

qa.q: How might Zubin see his six out of ten?
qa.a: Zubin seems relaxed and cheerful about it, treating mistakes as part of getting better.

grounding: Shows a child who cried over small errors and refused to hand in imperfect work, learning that mistakes are part of learning.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Avni, Wednesday.
During the letter-writing task, Avni erased the word "Dear" so many times that the page tore. She started again. By the end of the period, she had written only two lines and would not hand them in. "It's messy. It's all wrong."
When Irawati said, "Mine has mistakes too," Avni just shook her head and began to cry.
I knelt beside her and showed her my own lesson plan, full of crossings-out. "Mistakes are how we find out what to learn next."
What I'll do next: tomorrow I'll give the class "pencil-only drafts" with no erasers allowed, and I'll ask Avni to circle one mistake she's proud of finding.

qa.q: What did Avni erase so many times that the page tore?
qa.a: The word "Dear".

qa.q: How did Avni feel about her two lines, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt upset and ashamed of any flaw, calling it "messy" and "all wrong", refusing to hand it in and crying.

qa.q: How does the teacher's plan help Avni see mistakes differently?
qa.a: No-eraser drafts and circling a mistake she is proud of finding turn errors into a normal part of learning instead of failure.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been hoping for when she said "Mine has mistakes too"?
qa.a: Irawati was probably trying to comfort Avni and show her that mistakes are normal, and may have felt a bit helpless when Avni kept crying.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a child who erases until the paper tears and cries at small errors, and planning ways to show mistakes are part of learning.
